analysis.one_liner: Repeals the 15% minimum tax on the reported profits of corporations making over $1 billion.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the 15% corporate minimum tax on billion-dollar companies' reported profits never advanced past committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2022 Inflation Reduction Act created a 15% minimum tax on the profits that corporations with more than $1 billion in income report to their shareholders, designed so that very large companies cannot use deductions and credits to pay little or nothing. H.R. 3210 would repeal that tax entirely, backdated to tax years after 2022, removing the floor on what the biggest corporations owe. The bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote: it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and died there when the 118th Congress ended, with no cosponsors signed on.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the biggest winners would be the roughly 150 largest and most profitable US corporations subject to the tax — including major drug, tech, and defense companies — which would have owed less federal income tax on the profits they report to shareholders. Their shareholders and executives would benefit through higher after-tax returns.

how_it_helps.text: The bill strikes section 56A of the Internal Revenue Code, the 15% alternative minimum tax on the financial-statement (book) income of corporations with more than $1 billion in average annual profits, effective for tax years after 2022.

It also undoes related conforming provisions, including the corporate-level application of the general business credit limitation tied to the minimum tax, letting corporations use more credits against their tax bills.

analysis.who_pays: The lost revenue would be made up by other taxpayers, by cuts to public programs, or by larger federal deficits — costs borne by ordinary people and future generations.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the book minimum tax would again let the largest corporations deduct depreciation, credits, and other items immediately, so highly profitable companies could owe little or no federal income tax in years when they report billions in profit to shareholders — the gap the tax was designed to close.
Repeal would reduce federal revenue, meaning the tax burden shifts to other taxpayers or to future generations through borrowing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If it had passed, the benefit would have gone almost entirely to about 150 of the largest and most profitable US corporations, which would pay less tax on the profits they report to shareholders; the cost would have fallen on everyone else through either higher deficits or reduced public services. The bill offered no offsetting benefit to ordinary people, and its death preserved a tax that addresses a real gap — companies reporting large profits to investors while owing little federal tax.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it, so the bill died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced May 11, 2023, the bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, where it sat with no further action through the end of the 118th Congress.

The bill would have repealed the 15% corporate alternative minimum tax on the book income of companies reporting over $1 billion in profits, a tax enacted in 2022 to ensure the largest corporations pay at least some tax on reported profits.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest profitable corporations, which keep paying the 15% minimum tax on reported profits — the public keeps the revenue that would otherwise be lost, but no new help for ordinary people was produced either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public; the minimum tax stays

for.name: Rep. Jodey Arrington
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the 15% corporate book minimum tax

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican sponsor introduced the bill and no members of either party cosponsored it; the bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll-call record, but no Democratic support appeared.

industries.industry: Very large profitable corporations (over $1 billion in reported profits)
industries.note: The bill would repeal the 15% minimum tax on the profits these companies report to shareholders, letting some pay far less — or nothing — in federal income tax. Ordinary taxpayers would bear the lost revenue through higher deficits or cuts.
Compliance work created by the book minimum tax would disappear if it were repealed, reducing a revenue stream for firms that serve billion-dollar corporations.
